claim: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) affects the cerebellum and inferior olive.
source: The neurodegenerative disorder spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) affects the cerebellum and inferior olive, though previous research has focused primarily on the cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript.

claim: Previous research on SCA1 has focused primarily on the cerebellum.
source: The neurodegenerative disorder spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) affects the cerebellum and inferior olive, though previous research has focused primarily on the cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the literature review in the introduction.

claim: The molecular alterations present in the inferior olive in SCA1 are unknown.
source: As a result, it is unknown what molecular alterations are present in the inferior olive, and whether these changes are found in other affected tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract that the study addresses.

claim: Differentially regulated genes in the inferior olive segregate into several biological pathways in SCA1.
source: We found that differentially regulated genes in the inferior olive segregated into several biological pathways.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by pathway analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Vulnerable tissues in SCA1 are not uniform in their gene expression changes.
source: Comparison of the inferior olive and cerebellum demonstrates that vulnerable tissues in SCA1 are not uniform in their gene expression changes, and express largely discrete but some commonly enriched biological pathways.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by comparative transcriptomics data in the results.

claim: Brain-region-specific differences in SCA1 occur early in disease initiation and progression.
source: Importantly, we also found that brain-region-specific differences occur early in disease initiation and progression, and they are shared across the two mouse models of SCA1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by temporal analysis data at 5 and 12 weeks.

claim: Brain-region-specific differences in SCA1 are shared across two mouse models.
source: Importantly, we also found that brain-region-specific differences occur early in disease initiation and progression, and they are shared across the two mouse models of SCA1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by cross-model comparison data.

claim: Different mechanisms of degeneration are at work in the inferior olive and cerebellum in SCA1.
source: This suggests different mechanisms of degeneration at work in the inferior olive and cerebellum.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the observed differences in gene expression patterns between tissues.

claim: A large RNA-sequencing study in Huntington's disease mouse models identified gene clusters related to transcription, chromatin factors, and mitochondria that are specific to the striatum.
source: For example, a large RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) study conducted across brain regions and peripheral tissues in Huntington's disease (HD) mouse models identified gene clusters related to transcription, chromatin factors, and mitochondria that appear to be specific to the striatum (Langfelder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Langfelder et al., 2016).

claim: Glia-related genes were significantly enriched in the striatum and cortex as well as other tissues thought to be less affected in Huntington's disease.
source: The same study also found glia-related genes that were significantly enriched in the striatum and cortex, as well as other tissues thought to be less affected in HD, such as the cerebellum and brainstem (Langfelder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Langfelder et al., 2016).

claim: Regional variability in transcriptional changes were observed early in disease progression in Alzheimer's Disease, but similarities between tissues increased as animals aged.
source: In Alzheimer's Disease (AD), regional variability in transcriptional changes were observed early in disease progression, but the similarities between tissues increased as animals aged (Landel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Landel et al., 2014).

claim: A study in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 identified brain region-dependent variability in gene expression changes prior to the onset of motor phenotypes.
source: Finally, a recent study in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3) identified brain region-dependent variability in gene expression changes prior to the onset of motor phenotypes despite modest transcriptional alterations in brain regions that remain largely unscathed (Toonen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Toonen et al., 2018).

claim: SCA1 is characterized by impaired motor coordination and balance.
source: SCA1 is a fatal late-onset neurodegenerative disorder that is characterized by impaired motor coordination and balance (Globas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Globas et al., 2008).

claim: Atrophy and loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum and cell death in the inferior olive have been identified in postmortem SCA1 human tissue.
source: Atrophy and loss of Purkinje cells (PCs) in the cerebellum and cell death in the inferior olive have been identified in postmortem human tissue (Koeppen, 2005; Koeppen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Koeppen, 2005; Koeppen et al., 2013).

claim: Both the transgenic and knockin SCA1 mouse models demonstrate motor incoordination and Purkinje cell pathology.
source: Both SCA1 models demonstrate motor incoordination and PC pathology, and develop hallmark nuclear inclusions in PCs (Burright et al., 1995; Clark et al., 1997; Watase et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Burright et al., 1995; Clark et al., 1997; Watase et al., 2002).

claim: SCA1 is caused by a polyglutamine expansion in the ATAXIN-1 protein.
source: SCA1 is caused by a polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion in the ATAXIN-1 (ATXN1) protein, which is involved in gene regulation, including transcription (Orr et al., 1993).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Orr et al., 1993) and is established knowledge.

claim: ATXN1 is involved in gene regulation, including transcription.
source: SCA1 is caused by a polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion in the ATAXIN-1 (ATXN1) protein, which is involved in gene regulation, including transcription (Orr et al., 1993).
evidence: This is cited from prior research and supported by multiple studies on ATXN1 function.

claim: Capicua, SMRT, and RORa/Tip-60 have been shown to interact with ATXN1.
source: Transcriptional regulators, including Capicua, SMRT, and RORa/Tip-60, have been shown to interact with ATXN1 (Fryer et al., 2011; Gehrking et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2013b; Lam et al., 2006; Lim et al., 2008; Serra et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior research studies.

claim: Previous studies have investigated how polyQ-expanded ATXN1 impacts the normal transcriptional signature of the cerebellum.
source: Since ATXN1 functions as a transcriptional regulator, several previous studies have investigated how polyQ-expanded ATXN1 can impact the normal transcriptional signature of the cerebellum (Crespo-Barreto et al., 2010; Cvetanovic et al., 2011; Gatchel et al., 2008; Ingram et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2000; Serra et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior research studies.

claim: Glutamate signaling, calcium signaling, and long-term depression pathways are enriched in the SCA1 cerebellum at different time-points.
source: These studies have identified that various biological pathways, including glutamate signaling, calcium signaling, and long-term depression, are enriched in this tissue at different time-points (Crespo-Barreto et al., 2010; Gatchel et al., 2008; Ingram et al., 2016; Serra et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior research studies.

claim: The inferior olive has remained largely unstudied in SCA1 despite the prevalence of transcriptomic data from the cerebellum.
source: Despite the prevalence of transcriptomic data collected from the SCA1 cerebellum, other affected regions, such as the inferior olive, have remained largely unstudied.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap and motivation for the study.

claim: Neurons of the inferior olive send climbing fibers to innervate Purkinje cells.
source: Neurons of the inferior olive, a collection of subnuclei in the rostral medulla, send climbing fibers to innervate PCs (Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Bengtsson and Hesslow, 2006) and is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Purkinje cell axons synapse onto deep cerebellar nuclei, which send efferent fibers to various brain regions including the inferior olive.
source: PC axons, in turn, synapse onto deep cerebellar nuclei, which send efferent fibers to various brain regions including the inferior olive.
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Previous studies have found inferior olive cell loss in postmortem SCA1 human tissue.
source: Previous studies have found inferior olive cell loss in postmortem SCA1 human tissue, as well as changes in climbing fiber synaptic density on PCs (Koeppen et al., 2013; Kuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Koeppen et al., 2013; Kuo et al., 2017).

claim: Changes in climbing fiber synaptic density on Purkinje cells have been found in SCA1.
source: Previous studies have found inferior olive cell loss in postmortem SCA1 human tissue, as well as changes in climbing fiber synaptic density on PCs (Koeppen et al., 2013; Kuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Koeppen et al., 2013; Kuo et al., 2017).

claim: ATXN1-82Q transgenic mice exhibit aberrant climbing fiber pruning on Purkinje cell soma and dendrites.
source: These mice exhibit aberrant climbing fiber pruning on PC soma and dendrites, a reduction in the responsiveness of PCs to climbing fibers, and alterations in climbing fiber arborization and extension (Barnes et al., 2011; Duvick et al., 2010; Ebner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Barnes et al., 2011; Duvick et al., 2010; Ebner et al., 2013).

claim: Localization of ATXN1-82Q to the Purkinje cell nucleus is associated with alterations in climbing fiber-PC synapses.
source: Previous work has indicated that localization of ATXN1-82Q to the PC nucleus is associated with alterations in climbing fiber-PC synapses (Ebner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Ebner et al., 2013).

claim: Other neurodegenerative disorders including SCA7, 14, and 23, as well as Essential Tremor, have aberrant climbing fiber innervation on Purkinje cell soma and dendrites.
source: Other neurodegenerative disorders, including SCA7, 14, and 23, as well as Essential Tremor, have aberrant climbing fiber innervation on PC soma and dendrites, indicating that this observation is not isolated to SCA1 (Smeets and Verbeek, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Smeets and Verbeek, 2016).

claim: The molecular basis of inferior olive alterations in SCA1 is unknown.
source: Furthermore, the molecular basis of inferior olive alterations in SCA1 is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin and ATXN1-82Q transgenic mouse models faithfully recapture many aspects of the behavioral and pathological phenotypes associated with SCA1.
source: We used two SCA1 mouse models, knockin and PC-specific transgenic, which express polyQ-expanded ATXN1 in different cell types and tissues, but faithfully recapture many aspects of the behavioral and pathological phenotypes associated with SCA1 (Burright et al., 1995; Watase et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Burright et al., 1995; Watase et al., 2002).

claim: The defense response appears largely unique to the SCA1 inferior olive across SCA1 mouse models.
source: Particularly, the defense response appears largely unique to the SCA1 inferior olive across SCA1 mouse models.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by pathway analysis data.

claim: There are common and distinct enriched biological pathways between the SCA1 cerebellum and inferior olive.
source: We also found that there are common, and distinct, enriched biological pathways between the SCA1 cerebellum and inferior olive.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by comparative pathway analysis.

claim: Five weeks of age coincides with the earliest time-point of rotarod impairment in both Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin and ATXN1-82Q transgenic mouse models.
source: The first time-point selected for analysis was 5 weeks of age, which coincides with the earliest time-point of rotarod impairment in both mouse models (Clark et al., 1997; Watase et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Clark et al., 1997; Watase et al., 2002).

claim: The 12 week time-point coincides with the initiation of significant thinning of the molecular layer in ATXN1-82Q transgenic mice.
source: The 12 week time-point also coincides with the initiation of significant thinning of the molecular layer in ATXN1-82Q Tg mice, but precedes gross PC loss.
evidence: This is stated based on prior knowledge of the model's pathology.

claim: No gender-effects have previously been reported in SCA1 mouse models.
source: Since no gender-effects have previously been reported in SCA1 mouse models and to minimize potential gender-effects, if any, three male mice from each genotype were initially used for all RNA-seq experiments.
evidence: This is stated as justification for the experimental design based on prior knowledge.

claim: PolyQ-expanded Atxn1 is expressed in the inferior olive of Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin mice.
source: We first verified that polyQ-expanded Atxn1 is expressed in the inferior olive of Atxn1154Q/2Q KI mice (Figure 2A). A band corresponding to Atxn1-154Q was identified in the inferior olive as well as cerebellar extracts from Atxn1154Q/2Q KI mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 143 annotated transcripts were differentially regulated in the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive relative to wild-type controls.
source: RNA-seq in the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive identified 143 annotated transcripts differentially regulated relative to WT control littermates (FDR p-value < 0.05; n = 3 males per genotype) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 103 transcripts were up-regulated in the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: Of these 143 transcripts, 103 were up-regulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Response to organic substance, hormone metabolic process, and neuropeptide hormone activity were the top three biological pathway clusters significantly enriched in the 5 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: The top three biological pathway clusters that were significantly enriched in the Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive at 5 weeks were related to response to organic substance, hormone metabolic process, and neuropeptide hormone activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pathway analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 204 genes were differentially regulated in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive, with 43 up-regulated and 161 down-regulated.
source: In the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive, a total of 204 genes were differentially regulated, with 43 annotated transcripts up-regulated and 161 down-regulated (FDR p-value < 0.05; n = 3 males per genotype) (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Defense response was the most highly enriched pathway in the 12 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: Functional annotation clustering identified the defense response, which is the molecular response to a foreign body or injury, as the most highly enriched pathway in the 12 week old inferior olive (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pathway analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The defense response pathway in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive was composed of a large subset of interferon stimulated genes that were largely up-regulated.
source: The defense response pathway was composed of a large subset of ISGs, which were largely up-regulated (Figure 2E), and were validated using RT-qPCR (Figure 2F) (Irf7 p < 0.0001; Ifitm3 p = 0.0033; Oasl2 p < 0.0001; Stat1 p = 0.0003; t-test; n = 3 males per genotype).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq and RT-qPCR validation shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Irf7 was identified as the transcriptional regulator with the highest enrichment of downstream targets in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: IPA prediction for upstream regulators influencing gene expression changes identified Irf7 as the transcriptional regulator with the highest enrichment of downstream targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is a finding from IPA upstream regulator analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was significant enrichment for Irf7 binding site DNA motifs in up-regulated genes from the 12 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: This was confirmed after inputting inferior olive differentially regulated gene promoters into the MEME-suite FIMO application and assessing significant enrichment for Irf7 binding site DNA motifs relative to shuffled promoter sequences (Table 1) (Bailey et al., 2009; Grant et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from DNA motif analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of Iba1-positive cell soma in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive relative to wild-type controls.
source: Relative to WT control animals, there was a significant increase in the number of Iba1-positive cell soma in Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive (n = 3 males and females per genotype; p = 0.0488; t-test), but no significant change in Gfap fluorescence intensity at this time-point (n = 3 males and females per genotype; p > 0.05; t-test) (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: There was no significant change in Gfap fluorescence intensity in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive relative to wild-type controls.
source: Relative to WT control animals, there was a significant increase in the number of Iba1-positive cell soma in Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive (n = 3 males and females per genotype; p = 0.0488; t-test), but no significant change in Gfap fluorescence intensity at this time-point (n = 3 males and females per genotype; p > 0.05; t-test) (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: Irf7 mRNA expression was significantly up-regulated in BV2 microglial cells expressing human ATXN1-82Q.
source: The murine microglial BV2 cell line expressed significantly elevated levels of Irf7 mRNA following overexpression of human ATXN1-82Q (n = 4 wells per experimental group; p = 0.0145; t-test) (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a finding from cell culture experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: 62 annotated transcripts were altered in both the 5 week and 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive relative to wild-type controls.
source: Sixty-two annotated transcripts were altered in both the Atxn1154Q/2Q KI 5 week and 12 week inferior olive relative to their WT controls, making up approximately 43.4% of the 5 week differentially regulated gene list and 30.4% of the 12 week differentially regulated gene list (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: 29 genes were consistently up- or down-regulated across the 5 week and 12 week time-points in the Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: Among the 62 genes, 29 genes were consistently up- or down-regulated across time-points (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: 33 genes were dysregulated between the 5 week and 12 week time-points in the Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive.
source: The remaining 33 genes were dysregulated between the two time-points (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C). Those 33 genes were significantly up-regulated relative to WT controls at 5 weeks, then down-regulated relative to WT controls at 12 weeks of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: 25 annotated transcripts were differentially regulated in the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum compared to wild-type controls.
source: For the 5 week analysis, only 25 annotated transcripts were differentially regulated compared to WT controls (FDR p-value < 0.05; n = 3 males per genotype) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 943 genes were differentially expressed in the 12 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum, with 214 genes up-regulated and 729 genes down-regulated.
source: In the 12-week-old Atxn1154Q/2Q KI mice cerebella (Figure 3A), a total of 943 genes were differentially expressed, with 214 genes up-regulated and 729 genes down-regulated (FDR p-value < 0.05; n = 3 males per genotype) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Chemical synaptic transmission, transmembrane receptor activity, and gated channel activity were enriched pathways in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum.
source: Pathway enrichment for the entire cerebellar differentially expressed gene list revealed enrichment for pathways associated with chemical synaptic transmission, transmembrane receptor activity, and gated channel activity (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from pathway analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was strong enrichment for Cic binding site DNA motifs in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum among down-regulated genes.
source: Relative to shuffled nucleotide sequences, there was strong enrichment for Cic binding site DNA motifs in the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q KI cerebellum among down-regulated genes (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from DNA motif analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: There was enrichment among up-regulated inferior olive genes at 12 weeks of age for Cic binding sites, but the degree of enrichment was not as substantial as in the cerebellum.
source: There was enrichment among up-regulated inferior olive genes at 12 weeks of age for Cic binding sites, but the degree of enrichment was not as substantial as in the cerebellum (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from DNA motif analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: 17 genes overlapped between the 5 week and 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum differentially regulated gene lists.
source: Of the 25 genes differentially regulated in the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q KI cerebellum, 17 overlapped with the 12 week cerebellum dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: All genes significantly altered in both the 5 week and 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum were differentially regulated in the same direction.
source: In fact, all of the genes significantly altered in both the Atxn1154Q/2Q KI 5 week and 12 week cerebellum relative to appropriate WT controls were differentially regulated in the same direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: 14 genes overlapped between the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive and cerebellum, with 9 regulated in opposing directions.
source: In the 5 week old Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive and cerebellum comparison, 14 genes overlapped, 9 of which were regulated in opposing directions in each tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-tissue comparison analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 69 common genes were differentially regulated in both the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive and cerebellum, with 13 genes commonly up-regulated and 54 down-regulated.
source: In total, 69 common genes were differentially regulated in both tissues relative to appropriate WT controls, with 13 genes commonly up-regulated and 54 down-regulated (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-tissue comparison analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ATXN1-82Q mRNA is not significantly increased in the ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive relative to wild-type controls.
source: The ATXN1-82Q Tg mice exhibit robust overexpression of ATXN1-82Q mRNA in the cerebellum, but show no significant increase relative to WT control littermates in the inferior olive (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ATXN1-82Q protein is expressed in the cerebellum but does not resolve in the inferior olive of ATXN1-82Q transgenic mice.
source: Protein quantification of ATXN1-82Q found that, while it is expressed in whole cerebellar lysate, it does not resolve in the inferior olive (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 148 genes were differentially regulated in the 5 week old ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive relative to wild-type controls.
source: Analysis of RNA-seq data from 5 week old ATXN1-82Q Tg inferior olive identified 148 genes that were differentially regulated relative to their WT control littermates (FDR p < 0.05; n = 3 males per genotype) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 142 out of 148 genes were up-regulated in the 5 week old ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive.
source: The majority of genes (142 out of 148 genes) were up-regulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 126 genes were differentially regulated in the 12 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive.
source: The 12 week ATXN1-82Q Tg inferior olive RNA-seq data revealed 126 genes differentially regulated (FDR p-value < 0.05; n = 3 males per genotype) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Defense response was among the top ten pathways enriched in the 12 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive.
source: Interestingly, a cluster of pathways including defense response, regulation of defense response, cellular response to interleukin-I, and complement and coagulation cascade were among the top ten pathways enriched in the 12 week inferior olive (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 34 genes were commonly altered in both the ATXN1-82Q transgenic and Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin inferior olive at 12 weeks of age, with 33 commonly down-regulated.
source: In total, 34 genes were commonly altered in both the ATXN1-82Q Tg and the Atxn1154Q/2Q KI inferior olive relative to their WT controls at 12 weeks of age, with 33 of those genes commonly down-regulated (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-model comparison analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 12 defense response-related genes were commonly altered in the Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin and ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive at 12 weeks, with all commonly down-regulated.
source: A total of 12 defense response-related genes were commonly altered in each of the two groups out of a combined total of 101, with all of them commonly down-regulated (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-model comparison analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 402 genes were significantly different in the 5 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum relative to wild-type controls.
source: Sequencing in the 5 week ATXN1-82Q Tg mouse cerebellum revealed 402 genes significantly different relative to WT control littermates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: 350 genes were down-regulated in the 5 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum.
source: Of the 402 genes differentially regulated, 350 were down-regulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 1062 annotated transcripts were significantly altered in the 12 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum, with approximately 43% up-regulated.
source: A greater number of genes were significantly altered at the 12 week time-point, with 1062 annotated transcripts significantly altered in the ATXN1-82Q Tg cerebellum, with approximately 43% of genes up-regulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 323 genes were differentially regulated at both the 5 week and 12 week time-points in the ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum.
source: Between the two datasets, 323 genes were differentially regulated at both time-points relative to their WT controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: 316 out of 323 genes were regulated in the same direction across the 5 week and 12 week time-points in the ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum.
source: Interestingly, the majority of genes (316 out of the 323 genes) were regulated in the same direction (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C and C').
evidence: This is a finding from temporal comparison analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C and C'.

claim: 59 genes were commonly altered in both the 12 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic inferior olive and cerebellum.
source: At the 12 week time-point (Figure 6A), 59 genes were commonly altered in both tissues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-tissue comparison analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The majority of genes commonly altered in both the 12 week ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum and inferior olive were altered in opposing directions.
source: However, the majority of the genes commonly altered in both the 12 week ATXN1-82Q Tg cerebellum and inferior olive were altered in opposing directions, some of which were associated with cell growth and development (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-tissue comparison analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 316 genes overlapped between the 12 week Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin and ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum.
source: Of the genes altered in each tissue, a total of 316 genes overlapped (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-model comparison analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 177 genes were altered in opposing directions between the Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin and ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum at 12 weeks.
source: The directionality of these changes was largely discordant between mouse models, with 177 genes altered in opposing directions (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-model comparison analysis shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The majority of discordant genes between the two cerebellar models were down-regulated in the Atxn1154Q/2Q knockin cerebellum and up-regulated in the ATXN1-82Q transgenic cerebellum.
source: The majority of these discordant genes were down-regulated in the Atxn1154Q/2Q KI cerebellum and up-regulated in the ATXN1-82Q Tg cerebellum (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-model comparison analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Mouse and human ATXN1 show 89% identity and 92% positive substitution similarity in amino acid sequence lacking the polyQ tract.
source: Using NCBI Protein BLAST, mouse and human ATXN1 (NP_001186234 and NP_001121636, respectively) show 89% identity and 92% positive substitution similarity in amino acid sequence lacking the polyQ tract (Altschul et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis using NCBI Protein BLAST.

claim: Molecular layer thinning is obvious at 12 weeks in the ATXN1-82Q transgenic mouse model.
source: Molecular layer thinning is obvious at 12 weeks in the ATXN1-82Q Tg mouse model, but occurs at a later time-point in the Atxn1154Q/2Q KI mouse (Barnes et al., 2011; Clark et al., 1997; Duvick et al., 2010; Watase et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from prior research on the mouse models.
